newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: IRA said to rule out early truce.
newsitem.headline: IRA said to rule out early truce.

text.p: The Irish Republican Army was on Friday reported to have ruled out a new ceasefire in its war against British rule of Northern Ireland until after a British election due this year.
The Northern Ireland guerrilla organisation told correspondents from the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) and Ireland's RTE network that a new truce was "most unlikely".
"Our cessation of violence is off," a source close to the IRA leadership was quoted as telling journalists.
Asked about prospects for a ceasefire, the source said: "At the present there is no sign of a meaningful move from the British and in that event there is no immediate sign of a ceasefire."
It made its views known on the eve of the first anniversary of the IRA bombing of London's Canary Wharf complex which marked the end of an unprecedented 17-month IRA truce.
The guerrillas told journalists that a resolution of the 27-year Northern Ireland conflict required talks which included its political wing, Sinn Fein, without preconditions.
Britain has excluded Sinn Fein from the negotiations until the IRA declares a complete end to its hit-and-run war in a conflict which has killed 3,200.

The IRA restated its view that Britain had failed to seize the opportunity to get Sinn Fein involved in Belfast peace talks during the 17-month truce and said that it could not see any change in British attitudes until an election was held.

British Prime Minister John Major must call elections by May and the Irish government of Prime Minister John Bruton, London's partner in the peace process, is also due to hold an election by November this year.
The guerrillas denied allegations that they were trying to provoke retaliation by pro-British Loyalist guerrillas who called their own ceasefire in October 1994.

Security sources believe that the IRA wants to create mayhem in Northern Ireland so that the next British government has to take immediate steps to reach a political settlement and invite Sinn Fein to the negotiations.
The source said the IRA had "no desire for sectarian warfare to be resumed".
Loyalists have targeted members of the 40 per cent Catholic minority, from which the IRA draws support, in retaliation for IRA attacks.
Since October last year the IRA has switched the focus of its guerrilla war to Northern Ireland and has attacked security targets every week this year.
It has not killed anyone this year but the IRA source denied suggestions in the Irish media that it was conducting a "phoney war."
Loyalists have threatened to abandon their truce if the IRA kills anyone and police say they are taking the warning seriously.
